say: SwapPrint: quantum fingerprints for digital art. We start with Hokusai's Great Wave.
label: Artwork

say: Every 4x4 patch gets its own 11-qubit fingerprint state.
Now someone quietly edits the artwork: one pixel, one colour level.
Surprise me hides a single invisible edit somewhere in the image.
name: Surprise me

say: Can you spot the edit? Nobody can by eye.
Let's guess: click where we think the change is.
Press Verify: the SWAP test compares every fingerprint, tile by tile.
name: Verify

say: CHANGE DETECTED. The heatmap points straight at the edited tile.
Untouched tiles never fire. A changed tile fires about half the time.
Watch the SWAP test shots arrive one by one: grey is 0, magenta is 1.
name: ▶ Play shots

say: Why the encoding matters: same edit, same SWAP test, three encodings.
Switch to the textbook baseline encoding, FRQI.
label: Encoding

say: Verify again with FRQI...
name: Verify

say: NO CHANGE DETECTED. FRQI needs millions of shots to notice this edit.
Same SWAP test, different encoding: 99% detection takes 15.5 million shots with FRQI, 7 with ours.
How: tile, error-correcting code, 11-qubit sign state, SWAP test. One flipped bit flips about half the signs.
Measured, not assumed: 12 paintings, 3 stress images, 22 conditions, Wilson 95% intervals on sampled rates.
Honest limit: on a simulated IBM device noise model (FakeFez), identical states start to fire, so real devices need thresholds.
SHA-256 is still better in practice. What SwapPrint shows: the encoding decides what a SWAP test can see.
